findings.title: Second `self.downsize` definition silently overrides the 5-argument one
findings.body: Ruby has no method overloading, so the new `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149 replaces the earlier `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145. The first definition is dead code. Any existing caller using the width/height form with an options hash (5 arguments) now raises `ArgumentError`. A caller passing 4 arguments binds `max_height` to `opts`, and `opts[:allow_animation]` then fails. Keep one signature and update all callers, or give the percentage form a different name.

findings.title: Client-side size limit hard-coded to 10MB for all upload types
findings.body: `validateUploadedFile` used to read `max_image_size_kb` or `max_attachment_size_kb` from site settings, depending on `type`. It now uses a constant 10MB for both. The attachment limit is therefore ignored. If an admin sets it below 10MB, the client lets oversized files through and the server rejects them. If an admin sets it above 10MB, legitimate attachments are blocked on the client. The same hard-coded value is used in the 413 handler at line 246, so the error message no longer reports the real limit. Only images should get the 10MB cap, because the server now downsizes them. Attachments should keep using their setting.

findings.title: Downsizing uses the tempfile path, so the animated GIF branch is never taken and its arguments would be wrong
findings.body: `optimize` chooses the animated (gifsicle) variant only when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`. Rack and Tempfile paths have no extension, so an uploaded GIF never takes that branch. The static `convert from[0] -resize 80%>` path runs instead and flattens an animated GIF to its first frame, even with `allow_animation` enabled. If the branch were taken, `resize_instructions_animated` would emit `--resize-fit 80%`, which gifsicle does not accept (it takes `WxH`, or `--scale`). The in-place conversion also writes to an extensionless output path, so the output format is inferred and is not guaranteed for formats such as SVG. The code should work from the real filename or extension and handle GIFs explicitly.

findings.title: Return value of `downsize` ignored; failures retried 5 times and oversized file still used
findings.body: `OptimizedImage.downsize` returns false when `convert` fails, for example when the file is corrupt or the format is unsupported. The loop ignores that result and runs the same failing command up to 5 times. It then falls through to `Upload.create_for` with the original file. Break out of the loop when `downsize` returns false. Also note that five passes of 80% only shrink each dimension to about 33%, which may not be enough for very large files. Such files then fail with a generic size error.

findings.title: Hard-coded 10MB download cap and no server-side bound before running ImageMagick up to 5 times
findings.body: The API URL download limit changed from the configured `max_image_size_kb` to a literal `10.megabytes`. This is also used for non-image attachments. The only enforcement of the 10MB limit for direct uploads is the client JS, which is trivially bypassed. The server now runs `convert` up to 5 times, synchronously inside `Scheduler::Defer`, on whatever size and dimensions arrive. A user can upload a very large or decompression-bomb image and consume CPU and memory repeatedly. Enforce a server-side maximum input size (and ideally dimensions) before downsizing.

findings.title: No tests for the new auto-downsize behaviour or the changed OptimizedImage API
findings.body: The PR adds an auto-downsize loop in the uploads controller. It also changes the signatures of `OptimizedImage.resize`, `downsize` and `optimize` and removes `dimensions`. No tests were added or updated for any of it. The duplicate `downsize` definition would have been caught by a basic spec. Add specs for uploading an oversized image, for the setting set to 0, and for the `OptimizedImage` methods.
